hints: Focus on what happens when a Group 2 nitrate is heated strongly, and think about which products stay solid and which escape as gases.
The solid left behind weighs 5.00 - 3.29 = 1.71 g, so use the decomposition equation to link moles of nitrate to moles of oxide.
The mass lost per mole is always 108 g, so compare the percentage loss in the experiment with $108 / M_r$ of the nitrate to find the metal mass.
walkthrough:
**Write the decomposition equation**

All Group 2 nitrates decompose the same way on strong heating to the oxide, nitrogen dioxide and oxygen. Only the oxide stays as a solid.

$$2\text{M}(\text{NO}_3)_2 \rightarrow 2\text{MO} + 4\text{NO}_2 + \text{O}_2$$

**Find the mass of solid left**

The 3.29 g loss is the mass of the gases ($\text{NO}_2$ + $\text{O}_2$) that escape. The oxide residue stays behind.

$$\text{mass of MO} = 5.00 - 3.29 = 1.71 \text{ g}$$

**Link moles of nitrate to moles of oxide**

From the equation, 1 mol of $\text{M}(\text{NO}_3)_2$ gives 1 mol of $\text{MO}$. Let the metal atomic mass be $x$.

$$M_r[\text{M}(\text{NO}_3)_2] = x + 124$$
$$M_r[\text{MO}] = x + 16$$
$$\frac{5.00}{x+124} = \frac{1.71}{x+16}$$

**Solve for the metal and identify it**

Cross multiply and solve for $x$. This gives a value very close to 40, which is calcium.

$$5.00(x+16) = 1.71(x+124)$$
$$3.29x = 132.04$$
$$x \approx 40.1$$

options.A: Magnesium ($A_r = 24.3$) is too light. Its nitrate $M_r$ is about 148.3, so the fractional loss $108/148.3$ is about 73%, giving a loss of about 3.64 g from 5.00 g, larger than the observed 3.29 g.
options.B: Calcium ($A_r = 40.1$) fits perfectly. Calcium nitrate $M_r$ is 164.1 and calcium oxide $M_r$ is 56.1. Moles = 5.00/164.1 = 0.0305 mol, giving oxide mass 0.0305 x 56.1 = 1.71 g and loss 3.29 g, exactly as observed.
options.C: Strontium ($A_r = 87.6$) is too heavy. Its nitrate $M_r$ is about 211.6, so the fractional loss $108/211.6$ is only about 51%, giving a loss of about 2.55 g from 5.00 g, smaller than observed.
options.D: Barium ($A_r = 137.3$) is much too heavy. Its nitrate $M_r$ is about 261.3, so the fractional loss $108/261.3$ is only about 41%, giving a loss of about 2.07 g from 5.00 g, far smaller than observed.
